hints: Look closely at what was labelled here. It was the membrane proteins (red in human, green in mouse), not the lipids, and after 40 minutes the red and green mixed completely.
Ask yourself which model of membrane structure allows labelled proteins to drift sideways through the bilayer, and whether this applies to just surface proteins or also to spanning proteins.
walkthrough:
**Recall the famous fusion experiment**

This is the classic Frye and Edidin experiment. Think of it simply. Two cells with different coloured protein coats are joined into one big cell.

At first, one half is red and one half is green. After 40 minutes, red and green are mixed all over. That tells us the coloured proteins must have moved sideways.

**Apply the fluid mosaic model**

The fluid mosaic model says the membrane is fluid. Phospholipids form a flexible bilayer, and most proteins float in it like icebergs in the sea.

Because the bilayer is fluid, proteins can diffuse laterally between phospholipid molecules. They are not locked in one place.

**Check which proteins can move**

Both types of labelled protein mixed. That includes extrinsic proteins sitting in the outer layer and intrinsic proteins that span the whole bilayer.

So the correct explanation is that both outer layer proteins and spanning proteins can move freely between phospholipids. That is option D.

options.A: Incorrect, because if all proteins were fixed they could not mix. The red and green dyes did mix, so proteins must move.
options.B: Incorrect, because proteins and phospholipids do not move as fixed attached groups. They move independently within the fluid bilayer.
options.C: Incorrect, because it is too limited. Not only outer layer proteins move, spanning intrinsic proteins also diffuse laterally, as shown by complete mixing.
options.D: Correct, because the even mixing of red and green labels proves both extrinsic outer layer proteins and intrinsic spanning proteins can diffuse freely between phospholipids.
